This Tucker, Built After the Factory Closed, Sat Hidden for 13 Years, Great-Grandsons Bring It Home
17 photos
Photo: Preston Tucker's Speed Shop | YouTube
This 1948 Tucker was completed nearly 40 years after the Tucker factory permanently closed. Its body shell was stamped at the Chicago plant back in the late 1940s. The factory closed down in 1950, and the #1051 was not assembled into a finished, drivable car until the late 1980s.
The Tucker factory officially numbered its completed production cars sequentially from #1001 to #1050. Because Body #54 left the factory without an official chassis number, New Jersey car enthusiast and Air Force veteran Chick DeLorenzo, who had grown up in a Tucker dealership family, simply picked the very next number in sequence, #1051, when he finished building it in the late 1980s.
So the Tucker #1051 began as Body #54, one of eight unfinished car shells left behind when Preston Tucker's Chicago factory closed in 1949. Long story short, his build included a genuine, unused factory Tucker engine, which was originally a Franklin O-335 helicopter engine, and hand-crafted components.
After sitting hidden in a garage for 13 long years, it was bought in 2025 by Preston Tucker's great-grandsons, Mike and Sean, along with builder Rob Ida, finally bringing a factory-built Tucker body into the Tucker family.
Photo: Preston Tucker's Speed Shop | YouTube But it has been a bumpy road. After leaving the 1950 bankruptcy auction without a serial number, interior, or drivetrain, Body #54 passed through the hands of car collectors Ezra Schlipf of Metamora, Illinois, and Dewey Bloomquist of Sandwich, Illinois, before landing at the Poll Museum in Holland, Michigan.
For years, many assumed the bare shell was the missing factory car #1050, until factory body stampings proved it was actually Body #54. When Chick DeLorenzo acquired the unfinished car from the Poll Museum in 1986, it was a non-operational shell with loose hardware, delivered in bushel baskets. He simply refused to drop in a modern V8 and call it a day.
Instead, he tracked down a genuine leftover Franklin O-335 air-cooled helicopter engine converted to water-cooled by Tucker's engineers, engine #33584, the same powerplant Preston Tucker had adapted for the production cars, and paired it with a Cord pre-selector transmission.
Because exterior panels were extremely difficult to find, DeLorenzo molded his own fiberglass doors and fenders. For the wheel covers, he resorted to hand-spinning metal hubcaps on a lathe, pushing the metal against a form, leaving marks that are still visible today. He painted the car maroon over a tan interior after having been gray, red, and blue. It was August 1989 when he completed it.
Photo: Preston Tucker's Speed Shop | YouTube DeLorenzo passed away in January 2012, at the age of 76, and the car he completed spent years hidden in his garage in Butler, New Jersey. His family had tucked the Tucker #1051 away inside his Butler garage, where it remained unseen for 13 years. In the meantime, Preston Tucker's descendants had never owned a Tucker automobile .
In early 2025, his great-grandsons, Mike and Sean, teamed up with longtime family friend and custom car builder Rob Ida to purchase #1051 from the DeLorenzo family after keeping it tucked away for 13 years. The Tucker brothers got the call from the DeLorenzo family in December 2024. His daughter-in-law told them they were finally ready to let it go.
On pickup day , March 29, 2025, the team rolled the car into the sunlight for the first time since 2012. When Preston Tucker’s great-grandsons opened the front trunk of the Tucker #1051, they found a set of original vintage Tucker suitcases. Chick DeLorenzo had stored the set of custom Samsonite-style suitcases, complete with their original garment hangers, sold through the Tucker Accessories Program in 1948.
The trio trailered it to Ida's shop in Morganville, New Jersey. Without spark or fuel after such a long hibernation, the car was brought back to life, and the rear-mounted original Franklin engine roared again. They did everything that needed to be done to put the car back on the road.
Photo: Preston Tucker's Speed Shop | YouTube Since then, the Tucker has been exhibited at the Greenwich Concours d’Elegance on June 1, 2025, just two months after Preston Tucker's great-grandsons and Rob Ida pulled it out of its 13-year garage storage. The car was also spotted driving on the streets of New York City.
The Tucker #1051, tracked down by Preston Tucker’s great-grandsons, is not the last one built. There is also a Tucker #1052, formally cataloged as #1052C by the Tucker Automobile Preservation Society, which was completed in 2015.
Unlike #1051, which started as an unfinished factory body shell, #1052 was constructed around an original factory engineering test chassis, originally used to test Preston Tucker’s experimental automatic transmission in Chicago, using spare parts from several cars.
When Tucker's assets were liquidated in 1950, collector Ezra Schlipf also acquired this test chassis. In the following years, it passed through the hands of collectors. It was completed in 2015 and named "Sofie," after Preston Tucker’s mother.
